subject: Guidance on appropriate modeling framework, and model interpretation.

messages.author: f7b0e875c85b25ba
messages.subject: Guidance on appropriate modeling framework, and model interpretation.
parts:
Hi all, 

I have a couple questions regarding an analysis I recently begun, currently I am using pcountOpen but I am very open to suggestions. The overall question is related to developing estimates of annual raven abundance to use to address questions related to sage-grouse demographic processes. And the reason I am using an open population model is that I suspect migratory ravens are introducing a substantial amount of bias into our point count estimates, which I hope we can account for with the recruitment or survival parameters.

Background:

These data are collected from repeated point counts (specifically for ravens) along a transmission line corridor. Individual points are associated with 1 of 3 transects (South, Central, and North) and each transect contains 5 or 9 points (South = 5, Central and North = 9). Points are located approximately 5km from each other, and the nearest points among different transects are at least 15 km from each other). We conducted point count surveys for each transect 5-7 times each year for 10 years (except for one year where the grad student decided to only do 1 per transect). Point counts surveys were approximately 10 minutes long, and observed ravens were classified as either being within 400m of the transmission line, or beyond 400m. A survey consisted of 1 transect in a day, and we cycled through the timing and direction of the survey  (e.g., AM start from point 1, PM start from point 1, AM start from point 9, PM start from point 9). Surveys for each transect were approximately 10 days a part. 


Data format:
I have organized the data that each Year-Point is an independent unit, and originally each survey is a primary occasion (I then lumped two surveys together to create 4 primary occasions, with each primary consisting of 2 secondaries). Additionally, (and this is what I am really struggling with), I have separated out counts from our two distance classes (within and beyond 400m) as independent observations. So essentially, each point from each survey is psuedo-replicated to have two values, the raven count within 400m, and beyond.  Year, transect, and distance (within or beyond) are as site covariates (factors). Additionally, I have included 'primary' occasion as a yearlySiteCovs.


Questions:
1) Is there a more appropriate way to address this psuedo-replication issue that I have created? I could lump the observations into a single count, however I feel the heterogeneity in detection among the distance classes would be large.  I could also only consider count data from one of the distance classes. I don't think a distance sampling model is appropriate either, but I interested in hearing other people's thoughts.

2) Interpretation of including the primary occasion covariate on the recruitment parameter.  Am I interpreting this correctly that a gamma(primary occasion) model will provide occasion-specific (minus 1) estimates of 'entrance' into the population? In which, exp(gamma(Int)) = population growth from occasion 1 to 2, exp(gamma(Int+Primary1)) =  population growth from occasion 2 to 3, and so on? However, if I remove the primary occasion covariate, the model is still providing primary occasion specific estimates of lambda, but they are not allowed to vary by occasion?

3) The reported detection parameters are also primary occasion specific, correct? And the normal notation [1-(1-p1)*(1-p2)*(1-pn))] to calculate p* is appropriate? 



That's all I have for now.  Thanks in advance, and I apologize if any of these questions have been answered in detail previously.

-Dan

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Guidance on appropriate modeling framework, and model interpretation.
parts:
I would only use the data from <400m.  If you were interested in collapsing the data into an occupancy framework (which I'm not suggesting), you might find the >400m data useful.  But without an outer boundary defined, how can the counts be translated into a meaningful abundance or density?  I would assume most counted individuals are <400m anyway, and likely represent the bulk of the useful information here.

Yes, if primary occasion were used as a fixed effect on gamma, you are saying that each of the T-1 (with numPrimary = T) estimates of gamma can take its own value.  There are no primary occasion-specific estimates of lambda but you can derive estimates of N afterward using gamma and omega as specified in the help file.  To include the primary occasion as a covariate you need to make sure the MxT list for the yearlySiteCovs is specified as a factor.

Also, whether you use an "effects" or "means" parameterization will modify how the results are reported.  The default is an effects parameterization with an intercept and the difference of the additional fixed effects from that intercept (all on the logit scale).  If you subtract the intercept in your model specification, (~ x-1), then the mean estimates for each fixed effect are reported.  You cannot use a means parameterization if you have multiple categorical covariates for a given response variable (i.e., within the model for one of the probabilities).

All of this applies to detection probability as well, though for that you'll get T estimates if you make the primary occasion a fixed covariate.  I'm not sure what your p* notation is trying to convey.

Thanks Dan, 

Just to clarify the p* comment.  In standard robust design CMR frameworks that are comprised of a number of primary occasions which are in turn comprised of a number of secondary occasions, you are able to estimate a 'true' detection probability, denoted by p*, which is calculated for each primary occasion by (1-(1-detection in the first secondary occasion)*(1-detection in the second secondary occasion)* ..........(1-detection in the last secondary occasion)).  The basic premise is that as the population is closed within the primary, the overall detection within the primary should be a function of each of the secondaries. Does this concept translate into these models as well?

Thanks again for the help, it is much appreciated.

-Dan

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Guidance on appropriate modeling framework, and model interpretation.
parts:
Well, if p is the probability that an event occurs then p* = 1-(1-p)^K is the probability that an event occurs at or before K.  This applies beyond capture-recapture or occupancy, but yes it is useful for understanding the probability of ever capturing an individual or species if you have K total surveys.

But we have to be clear on what p is representing.  For an N-mixture model (as in pcountOpen), p is the probability of detecting an individual during a single survey.  So your original notation for p* could have referred to 1) the probability of detecting ANY individual, given K individuals at a site, or 2) the probability of EVER detecting a certain individual, given K surveys at a site.  The first one requires that you know the true number of individuals at the site (here K, but more commonly N), so it might be most useful for simulating data.  It is also helpful for understanding the relationship between the counts and the estimates of N.

It seems you're interested in p* across secondary occasions, so the second explanation is more applicable here.  And you are correct in that the equation for p* needs to be modified if p is occasion-specific: 1 - (1-p[1])*(1-p[2])*...(1-p[K]), where p[k] is the occasion-specific p.
